source_text: Ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ τοῖς γεγαμηκόσι παραινέσαιμι ἂν οἴκοι τὰς γυναῖκας τὰς σφῶν μήποτε κατὰ πρόσωπον οἰκετῶν φιλεῖν. οὐδὲ γὰρ προσγελᾶν δούλοις Ἀριστοτέλης εἴα ποτέ, πολλοῦ γε καὶ δεῖ κατ᾿ ὄψιν αὐτῶν φιλοφρονούμενον φαίνεσθαι τὴν γυναῖκα. ἄμεινον δὲ οἴκοθεν ἀρξαμένους ἀπὸ τοῦ γάμου τὴν σεμνότητα ἐπιδείκνυσθαι. μεγίστη γὰρ ἡ σωφροσύνης συζυγία καθαρᾶς ἡδονῆς ἀποπνέουσα. πάνυ γοῦν θαυμασίως ἡ τραγῳδία. φεῦ φεῦ, γυναῖκες, (φησίν) ὡς ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἄρα οὐ χρυσός, οὐ τυραννίς, οὐ πλούτου χλιδὴ τοσοῦτον εἶχε διαφόρους τὰς ἡδονὰς ὡς ἀνδρὸς ἐσθλοῦ καὶ γυναικὸς εὐσεβοῦς γνώμη δικαία καὶ φρονοῦσα τἄνδικα. ταῦτα τῆς δικαιοσύνης τὰ παραγγέλματα καὶ παρὰ τοῖς τὴν κοσμικὴν μετιοῦσι σοφίαν ἐκφωνηθέντα οὐ παραιτητέον. ἐγνωκότες οὖν »τὸ ἑκάστου ἔργον, ἐν φόβῳ τὸν τῆς παροικίας ὑμῶν χρόνον ἀναστράφητε, εἰδότες ὅτι οὐ φθαρτοῖς, ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ, ἐλυτρώθημεν ἐκ τῆς ματαίας ἡμῶν ἀναστροφῆς πατροπαραδότου, ἀλλὰ τιμίῳ αἵματι ὡς ἀμνοῦ ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου Χριστοῦ.« »ἀρκετὸς οὖν ὁ παρεληλυθὼς χρόνος,« ὁ Πέτρος φησί, »τὸ βούλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν κατειργάσθαι, πεπορευμένους ἐν ἀσελγείαις, ἐπιθυμίαις, οἰνοφλυγίαις, κώμοις, πότοις καὶ ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις.« ὅρον ἔχωμεν τὸν σταυρὸν τοῦ κυρίου, ᾧ περισταυρούμεθα καὶ περιθριγκούμεθα τῶν προτέρων ἁμαρτιῶν. ἀναγεννηθέντες τοίνυν προσηλωθῶμεν [ἐν] τῇ ἀληθείᾳ καὶ ἀνανήψωμέν τε καὶ ἁγιασθῶμεν, »ὅτι οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ κυρίου ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ὦτα αὐτοῦ εἰς δέησιν αὐτῶν, πρόσωπον δὲ κυρίου ἐπὶ ποιοῦντας κακά. καὶ τίς ὁ κακώσων ἡμᾶς, ἐὰν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ζηλωταὶ γενώμεθα;« ἡ δὲ ἀρίστη ἀγωγὴ εὐταξία ἐστίν, παντελὴς οὖσα εὐσχημοσύνη καὶ δύναμις τεταγμένη βεβαία, τῶν ἑξῆς ἀλλήλοις κειμένων ἐν ἔργῳ καλῶς ἀποδοτική, κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν ἀνυπέρβλητος. Ταῦτα, εἰ καὶ τραχύτερον προηνέχθην οἰκονομούμενος τῆς ἐπανορθώσεως τὴν σωτηρίαν, ἐμοὶ μὲν λελέχθων, φησὶν ὁ παιδαγωγός, ἐπειδὴ »ὁ ἐλέγχων μετὰ παρρησίας εἰρηνοποιεῖ,« ὑμεῖς δὲ εἰ μὲν ἀκούσεσθέ μου, σωθήσεσθε, εἰ δ᾿ οὐ προσέξετε τοῖς εἰρημένοις, οὔ μοι μέλει· μέλει δὲ ὅμως καὶ οὕτως· »τὴν γὰρ μετάνοιαν τοῦ ἁμαρτωλοῦ μᾶλλον ἢ τὸν θάνατον αἱρεῖται.« »ἢν δὲ εἰσακούσητέ μου, τὰ ἀγαθὰ τῆς γῆς φάγεσθε«, ὁ παιδαγωγὸς πάλιν λέγει, γῆς ἀγαθὰ τὰ ἀνθρώπεια ὀνομάζων καλά, τὸ κάλλος, τὸν πλοῦτον, τὴν ὑγίειαν καὶ τὴν ἰσχύν, τὴν τροφήν· ἀγαθὰ μὲν γὰρ ὄντως »ἃ οὔτε οὖς ἤκουσεν οὔτε ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνέβη ποτέ«, περὶ τὸν ὄντως ὄντα βασιλέα τὰ ὄντως ὄντα ἀγαθὰ ὄντα καὶ ἀναμένοντα ἡμᾶς· ἀγαθῶν γάρ ἐστι καὶ δοτὴρ καὶ φύλαξ· κατὰ μετουσίαν δὲ ἐκείνων τὰ τῇδε συνωνυμεῖ, παιδαγωγοῦντος ἐνθέως τοῦ λόγου τὴν ἀνθρώπων ἀσθένειαν ἀπὸ τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἐπὶ τὴν νόησιν. Ὅσα μὲν οὖν οἴκοι παραφυλακτέον καὶ ὡς τὸν βίον ἐπανορθωτέον, ὁ παιδαγωγὸς ἡμῖν ἅδην διείλεκται· ἃ δ᾿ οὖν καὶ κατὰ τὰς ὁδοὺς ὁμιλεῖν αὐτῷ φίλον τοῖς παιδίοις ἄχρις ἂν ἀγάγῃ αὐτὰ πρὸς τὸν διδάσκαλον, ταῦτα δὲ ἡμῖν ἐν κεφαλαίου μέρει δι᾿ αὐτῶν ὑποτίθεται καὶ παρατίθεται τῶν γραφῶν, γυμνὰς παρατιθέμενος τὰς παραγγελίας, ἁρμοζόμενος μὲν τῷ χρόνῳ τῆς καθοδηγήσεως, τὰς δὲ ἐξηγήσεις αὐτῶν ἐπιτρέπων τῷ διδασκάλῳ· καὶ γὰρ ὁ νόμος αὐτοῦ τὸν φόβον ὑπεκλύειν βούλεται τὸ ἑκούσιον ἐλευθερώσας εἰς πίστιν.
pass_a_gloss: I would advise even those who are married to love their wives at home, not in the presence of servants. For not even Aristotle allowed slaves to be fondly regarded, and it is necessary for the wife to be seen as being kindly disposed towards them. But it is better for those who have begun from marriage to show dignity at home. For the greatest marriage is the one of chastity, breathing pure pleasure. The tragedy says, 'Alas, alas, women,' that among humans, neither gold nor tyranny nor wealth's indulgence has as many different pleasures as the opinion of a good man and a pious woman, a just and manly thinking. These are the commands of righteousness, and they have been spoken not only by those who possess worldly wisdom, but also by us, and they should not be rejected. Having known, therefore, 'each one's work, in fear spend the time of your sojourning, knowing that we were redeemed from our vain conversation, inherited from our fathers, not with perishable things, with silver or gold, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and spotless, Christ.' 'The past time is enough,' Peter says, 'to have done the will of the Gentiles, having walked in lasciviousness, desires, wine-drinkings, revelings, drinkings, and unlawful idolatries.' Let us have as a boundary the cross of the Lord, by which we are crucified and put to death to our former sins. Having been reborn, therefore, let us be devoted to the truth and let us be raised and sanctified, 'for the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and His ears are open to their prayer, and the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. And who will harm us if we become zealous for what is good?' The best upbringing is self-control, being complete modesty and a steadfast power, with the things that follow being well-arranged and placed in order, unbeatable in virtue. These things, even if they were spoken more roughly, being managed for the sake of correction and salvation, 'he who rebukes with frankness makes peace,' the Pedagogue says. If you listen to me, you will be saved; but if you do not pay attention to what has been said, I do not care; yet I do care: 'for repentance of the sinner is chosen rather than death.' 'If you listen to me, you will eat the good things of the earth,' the Pedagogue says again, calling human goods 'good things,' beauty, wealth, health, and strength, nourishment; for the things that 'neither ear has heard nor has arisen in the heart' are truly good, concerning the truly existing King, the truly existing good things that are waiting for us; for He is the giver and guardian of good things. According to participation, however, the things that are named here are synonymous, the Word pedagogically guiding human weakness from the senses to the intellect. The Pedagogue has, therefore, spoken to us about the things that must be guarded at home and how to correct our life. The things that are also pleasant for the children to converse about on the roads until they are led to the teacher, these are proposed and presented to us in the headings of the Scriptures, placing the commands nakedly, fitting the time of guidance, and entrusting the explanations of them to the teacher; for his law also wants to overshadow fear, having freed the voluntary for faith.

pass_b_english: I would advise even married men to show affection for their wives at home, not in the presence of servants. Aristotle did not even allow slaves to be treated with fond familiarity, and it is all the more necessary that a wife not appear to be kindly disposed toward them in that setting. It is better, rather, for those who begin from marriage to display dignity at home; for the union of chastity is the greatest marriage, breathing pure pleasure. The tragedy cries out beautifully: "Alas, alas, women," it says, "among humans neither gold, nor tyranny, nor the indulgence of wealth has so many varied pleasures as the judgment of a good man and a pious woman, just and right-minded." These are the commands of righteousness, and they have been proclaimed even among those who practice worldly wisdom; they must not be rejected. Therefore, knowing "that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot," conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile (1 Peter 1:17-19). "The time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry" (1 Peter 4:3). Let us make the cross of the Lord our boundary, by which we are crucified and put to death to our former sins. Having been born again, therefore, let us devote ourselves to the truth and let us become sober and be sanctified; "for the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil." "And who will harm you if you are zealous for what is good?" (1 Peter 3:12-13). The best upbringing is self-control, being complete decorum and a steadfast, ordered power, arranging the things that follow well in their work, and unsurpassed in virtue.

The Pedagogue says these things, even if they were spoken somewhat roughly, because he manages them for the sake of correction and salvation: "He who rebukes with frankness makes peace." If you listen to me, you will be saved; but if you do not pay attention to what has been said, I do not care—yet I do care even so: "For He prefers the repentance of the sinner rather than his death." "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land," the Pedagogue says again, calling human goods "good things"—beauty, wealth, health, strength, nourishment. For the things that "no ear has heard, nor has it entered the heart of man" are truly good, concerning the truly existing King, the truly existing good things that exist and await us; for He is both giver and guardian of good things. By participation, however, the things here are named synonymously, the Word pedagogically guiding human weakness from the senses to the intellect. The Pedagogue has therefore fully discoursed to us about what must be guarded at home and how life must be corrected. As for the things that are also pleasant for the children to converse about on the roads until He leads them to the Teacher, these He proposes and sets before us in the headings of the Scriptures, laying down the commands plainly, suiting the time of guidance, and entrusting their explanations to the Teacher; for His law also wishes to dispel fear, having freed the voluntary will for faith.

review.notes: Pass A fails on agency and meaning in the first sentence: the Greek 'τὰς γυναῖκας τὰς σφῶν μήποτε κατὰ πρόσωπον οἰκετῶν φιλεῖν' means 'to love one's own wives not in the presence of servants', whereas Pass A translates it as 'to love their wives at home, not in the presence of servants' (adding 'at home' to the clause where it belongs to the location of the action, but more importantly, the Greek 'οἰκετῶν' refers to the servants, not the location of the love). Pass B correctly identifies the agency. However, Pass A fails on the translation of 'φιλοφρονούμενον φαίνεσθαι τὴν γυναῖκα' as 'it is necessary for the wife to be seen as being kindly disposed towards them [the slaves]', whereas the Greek indicates the husband should make it appear that the wife is kindly disposed towards the slaves (the wife is the object of the appearance). Most critically, Pass A fails the scripture requirement: it omits the required inline citations for the 1 Peter passages which are present in the Greek and Pass B. Pass B includes them, but Pass A does not. Furthermore, Pass A translates 'ἀναστράφητε' as 'spend the time', while the Greek 'ἀναστράφητε' (conduct yourselves/live) is a verb of action, not just time. Pass A also translates 'ἀναψῶμεν τε καὶ ἁγιασθῶμεν' as 'let us be raised and sanctified', whereas 'ἀναψῶμεν' (from ἀναψύχω) means 'to be refreshed/revived', not 'raised' (which would be ἀναστῶμεν or similar).
reasons: Pass A fails to provide the required inline scripture citations for the 1 Peter quotes present in the Greek text.
Pass A translates 'ἀναψῶμεν' (to be refreshed/revived) as 'be raised', which is a semantic error.

Pass A translates 'τὰς γυναῖκας... φιλεῖν' in a way that obscures the relationship between the husband, wife, and servants compared to the Greek 'τὰς γυναῖκας τὰς σφῶν μήποτε κατὰ πρόσωπον οἰκετῶν φιλεῖν'.
